findings.title: Google credential key is overwritten with the Zod SafeParse wrapper object instead of the token data
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the Zod `safeParse` result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed credentials. In the Google refresh path the whole result is assigned to `key` and then persisted via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. After the first token refresh, the stored credential key becomes `{success: true, data: {access_token,...}}`, and the next instantiation of `GoogleCalendarService` fails at `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` (no top-level `access_token`/`refresh_token`), breaking Google Calendar for that user until they reconnect. Previously the code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` directly. Use `.data` (or return the data from the helper).

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: The new refresh block in `getClient` calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (imports are only jsforce, rrule, zod, lib helpers and types). This is a type-check error and, if it slipped through, a `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime on every Salesforce service instantiation, making the Salesforce integration unusable.

findings.title: Helper injects a literal `refresh_token: "refresh_token"` that can overwrite the real refresh token in the DB
findings.body: When the parsed token response lacks `refresh_token`, the helper unconditionally sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. This runs in the normal (non-sync) path too. In `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` the schema declares `refresh_token` as optional and the result is spread over the stored credentials (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`) and persisted. If Microsoft omits `refresh_token` from a refresh response, the user's real refresh token is replaced with the string "refresh_token" in the database, and every subsequent refresh fails permanently (user must reconnect). Before this PR an absent key simply left the existing refresh token intact. The placeholder should not be written when a real value exists / the field is absent.

findings.title: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses computed keys that evaluate to "[object Object]", so it strips every field except access_token
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are computed property keys that both evaluate to the string "[object Object]" (the second overriding the first). The resulting schema is effectively `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`. Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, so in credential-sync mode `data` contains only `access_token`: `expires_in`/`expiry_date`, `instance_url`, `scope`, etc. are all dropped. Consequences: Zoom computes `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = NaN (serialized as null, failing `zoomTokenSchema` on the next call); Office365 loses `expires_in` so the token is treated as expired on every request; Salesforce loses `instance_url` so the next `jsforce.Connection` has no instance URL. The intent ("allow other properties") requires `.passthrough()` or `z.record`, not computed keys.

findings.title: Sync path returns a raw fetch `Response`, but several callers expect SDK-shaped results (hubspot token object, gaxios/axios `.data`)
findings.body: When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` regardless of what the wrapped `refreshFunction` would have returned. Callers were written against the original SDK shapes: `hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts` treats the result as a `HubspotToken` (`.expiresIn`, `.accessToken`) and persists it—storing a `Response` object (serialized as `{}`) as the credential key and calling `setAccessToken(undefined)`; `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` reads `res.data.access_token` (a `Response` has no `.data`, so this throws a TypeError); `zoho-bigin` and `zohocrm` read `tokenInfo.data.error` from what they expect to be an axios response, which throws. `larkcalendar` passes it to `handleLarkError` expecting Lark's `{code, data}` envelope. The comment says the endpoint response "should only contain the access token and expiry date", but each adapter needs a different shape, so no single self-hosted endpoint can satisfy them. The helper needs per-adapter normalization (e.g. return parsed JSON and let adapters map it) rather than a shared raw Response.

findings.title: Request to the self-hoster's credential sync endpoint carries no authentication
findings.body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body with no secret/signature header (e.g. `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` under `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`, which the inbound webhook already requires). The endpoint returns live OAuth access tokens for arbitrary user ids, so the self-hoster is forced to either leave it unauthenticated (anyone who can reach it can obtain any user's third-party tokens by guessing numeric ids) or rely on network-level controls. The outgoing request should include the shared secret so the endpoint can verify the caller.

findings.title: zoho-bigin passes `credentialId` where `refreshOAuthTokens` expects the user id
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential's id as the third argument, which the helper documents and uses as `userId` (sent as `calcomUserId` to the sync endpoint). In sync mode the self-hoster's endpoint would receive a credential id masquerading as a user id and return tokens for the wrong user (or none). Every other adapter passes `credential.userId`; this one should too (and `refreshAccessToken` needs access to the credential's userId, which it currently doesn't receive).

findings.title: Zoom sends app slug "zoomvideo" to the sync endpoint, but the app's slug is "zoom"
findings.body: The inbound webhook (`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`) looks apps up by their store slug, and Zoom's slug is `zoom` (see `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts` creating the credential with `appId: "zoom"`). The refresh path, however, calls `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", ...)`. A self-hoster keying their endpoint by the same slugs they use for the webhook will not recognize `zoomvideo`, so Zoom token refresh via sync fails. Use the canonical slug `zoom` to match the rest of the system.

findings.title: Webhook upserts by (userId, appId) and will silently overwrite an arbitrary credential when a user has several for the same app
findings.body: Cal.com allows multiple credentials per user for the same app (e.g. several Google Calendar accounts, each a separate `Credential` row with `appId: "google-calendar"`). The handler does `findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` with no ordering and overwrites whichever row is returned, so a sync for one connected account can clobber the keys of a different one, breaking that calendar connection. It also never considers team-owned credentials. The payload should identify the target credential (e.g. a credential id or an external account identifier), or the handler should refuse/branch when more than one match exists.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with `!==` and no HTTP method/body-shape error handling
findings.body: The shared secret header is compared with plain `!==`, which is not constant-time and leaks timing information about the secret; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. The handler also accepts any HTTP method (a GET with a header would try to `parse(req.body)` and throw) and lets `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse`, `symmetricDecrypt`, and `JSON.parse` throw unhandled, producing 500s with stack details instead of a 400. Restrict to POST and wrap validation/decryption in proper error responses.

findings.title: Salesforce now refreshes the token and writes the DB on every service instantiation, and still connects with the old access token
findings.body: `getClient` unconditionally POSTs to `login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and performs a `prisma.credential.update` every time `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed (which happens for every booking/availability flow), regardless of whether the stored token is still valid—previously jsforce refreshed lazily. This adds a network round-trip and a DB write per instantiation and will hit Salesforce token-endpoint rate limits. Moreover, the `jsforce.Connection` is still built with `credentialKey.access_token` / `credentialKey.instance_url` (the pre-refresh values) rather than `accessTokenParsed.data`, so the freshly obtained token isn't even used. Also `response.statusText !== "OK"` is fragile (HTTP/2 responses have an empty statusText); check `response.ok`.

findings.title: Helper throws on invalid response, making callers' `!success` branches dead and changing Office365 error behavior
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws `"Invalid refreshed tokens were returned"` when validation fails, so the `if (!parsedToken.success)` checks in `zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts` and `salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts` can never execute. For Office365 this silently changes behavior: the previous code logged the Zod error together with Microsoft's raw response and continued; now the diagnostic logging was deleted and the refresh throws, leaving operators with no information about why Microsoft's response was rejected. Either return the failed result and let callers handle it, or keep the diagnostic logging in the helper.

findings.title: No tests for the new webhook or the shared refresh helpers
findings.body: The PR adds a new authenticated API endpoint that writes third-party credentials to the DB and two helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that are now on the token-refresh path of ten integrations, yet ships no unit or integration tests (the PR checklist explicitly says none were added). Several of the defects above (SafeParse wrapper stored as key, broken computed-key schema, Response vs SDK shape mismatch, missing prisma import) would have been caught by even a basic test of each helper's output shape and of one adapter's refresh flow in both sync and non-sync modes.
